meta.title: Robust Flood Extent Mapping with Gated Fusion of Multi-Temporal and Multimodal Sentinel Observations

abstract: Rapid flood extent mapping from satellite imagery is critical for disaster response, yet operational settings rarely provide a complete and perfectly synchronized set of observations. Existing fusion approaches typically combine Sentinel-1 (S1) and Sentinel-2 (S2) acquisitions observed close in time to the flood event, which limits their ability to exploit historical context and makes them sensitive to missing modalities. We propose a multimodal framework for flood extent mapping that uses one mandatory flood-time S1 image together with optional auxiliary modalities: flood-time S2, pre-flood S1, and pre-flood S2. Each modality is encoded with a remote-sensing foundation model, to obtain a common embedding space. A lightweight context generator produces a shared context embedding, which is concatenated with each modality embedding and processed by a gating network. The resulting gates are used to compute a weighted average over the available modality embeddings before decoding into a binary flood mask. The aggregation is permutation-invariant and naturally handles missing inputs. Experiments on a subset of the Kuro Siwo dataset with added Sentinel-2 images, show that the proposed design effectively leverages multimodal and multi-temporal observations while remaining robust when auxiliary modalities are unavailable.

blocks.html: Flood extent mapping from Earth observation imagery is a key component of disaster management. Sentinel-1 SAR is particularly valuable because it is weather-independent and available day and night, while Sentinel-2 provides complementary optical information whenever cloud conditions allow. Recent remote-sensing foundation models like SMAR- TIES [1] further enable a common feature space across heterogeneous sensors, opening the door to more flexible fusion strategies. In parallel, the Kuro Siwo benchmark has highlighted the importance of large-scale, multi-temporal flood datasets for evaluating modern flood mapping systems [2].

Most multimodal flood mapping approaches fuse a flood-time S1 image with the nearest available S2 image [3, 4]. While effective when both observations exist, such methods do not fully exploit historical observations acquired before the event and are brittle when some modalities are absent. In practice, pre-flood images often contain useful contextual cues about permanent water, land cover, and background appearance, and missing modalities are common in operational workflows. An exception to this is OmbriaNet [5] which is both multimodal and bi-temporal. It is however not robust to missing modalities, limiting its applicability in operational settings.

We address this setting with a robust multimodal architecture that requires only a flood-time S1 image and can optionally use flood-time S2, pre-flood S1, and pre-flood S2. The method combines a shared context representation with pixel-wise modality gating, enabling adaptive fusion at each spatial location. The final aggregation is related in spirit to permutation-invariant set processing [6], which makes the design naturally suited to variable modality availability.

which produces a shared context embedding C. For each modality, a pixel-wise gating network receives the concatenation of the modality embedding and the shared context, and predicts a gate map

blocks.html: where ⊙denotes element-wise multiplication and ϵ is a small constant for numerical stability. The fused feature map F is then decoded by a standard UperNet [7] into a binary flood segmentation mask.

Two design choices are central. First, the shared SMAR- TIES embedding space makes it possible to process heterogeneous sensors within a common backbone [1]. Second, the aggregation in Equation (4) is permutation-invariant with respect to the set of available modalities, which connects the model to Deep Sets-style processing of unordered inputs [6]. This allows to handle missing modalities gracefully or even include multiple images of the same modality (for example multiple pre-flood S2). To improve robustness, the model is trained with modality dropout, i.e. optional modalities are randomly removed during training so that the network learns to rely on any informative subset. An overview of the architecture is shown in Figure 1.

The experiments were conducted on a subset of the Kuro Siwo S1 data set [2] for which S2 images with less than 50% cloud cover could be found in a 24 h window around the S1 observation. For this subset, corresponding Sentinel- 2 imagery (1 flood-time and 2 pre-flood) were generated through the OpenEO framework [8]. Both S2 (Blue, Green, Red, Nir, SWIR1 and SWIR2) and S1 (VV, VH) were resampled to 10m resolution. The result is a set of over 2000 patches from 10 different events containing flood-time and pre-flood images from both S1 and S2. We evaluate the proposed framework in realistic multimodal settings where varying input sets may be absent. In contrast to conventional S1–S2 fusion based only on flood-time observations, the proposed model can additionally exploit pre-flood imagery for both modalities, providing additional context.

To evaluate the contribution of the gating mechanism, we compare the proposed architecture against two alternative fusion strategies. In the Pool baseline, embeddings from all available modalities are simply averaged before decoding. In the Stacked baseline, modality embeddings are concatenated channel-wise and directly fed to the Uper- Net decoder, leading to a separate model architecture for every input modality combination. The proposed method instead performs pixel-wise gated fusion of modality embeddings prior to decoding, allowing to handle every set of input modalities within the same model. Table 1 reports the intersection-over-union (IoU) for the water class for different combinations of flood-time and pre-flood modalities. Across most modality configurations, the proposed gating mechanism achieves the best or tied-best mIoU. However, the absolute differences compared with average pooling and stacking are modest, typically within a few tenths of an IoU point. We therefore interpret these results primarily as evidence that the proposed fusion mechanism preserves competitive segmentation accuracy while supporting a variable set of input modalities within a single model.

When heterogeneous modalities are combined, gated fusion provides small but consistent improvements in several configurations. For example, using flood-time S1 together with pre-flood S2 yields an mIoU of 88.8, compared with 88.4 for average pooling and 88.5 for stacking. While these differences are limited in magnitude, they indicate that adaptive weighting does not compromise performance while providing additional flexibility in how available observations are combined.

blocks.html: Qualitative experiments show that the pixel-wise gating mechanism adapts to spatially varying evidence from different modalities. Flood-time S1 remains the core source of information, while optional flood-time and pre-flood observations contribute when informative as seen in Figure 2. The architecture remains operational when only the essential flood-time S1 image is present, and performance degradation under missing auxiliary modalities is limited. This behaviour is particularly relevant for emergency response, where cloud cover, revisit mismatches, and data availability constraints make complete modality sets uncommon.

The proposed framework extends flood extent mapping beyond rigid pairwise S1–S2 fusion by treating multimodal, multi-temporal observations as an optional set around one essential S1 input. This formulation is operationally attractive because it matches how data actually arrive during flood events: asynchronously, incompletely, and with varying utility across space.

The experimental results demonstrate that the proposed gated fusion strategy can outperform simpler aggregation approaches. While average pooling already provides a strong baseline, the learned gating mechanism enables the model to adaptively emphasize the most informative modalities for each pixel.

The comparison with the stacked baseline further highlights the importance of structured fusion. Directly concatenating modality embeddings increases the decoder input dimensionality (and model size) but does not explicitly model the relative importance of each modality. In contrast, the proposed gating mechanism learns pixel-wise relevance weights, enabling a single model to selectively combine observations from different sensors and acquisition times.

The relatively small differences between fusion strategies suggest that improved peak segmentation accuracy is not the main advantage of the proposed architecture. Rather, its key benefit is the ability to use one unified model across a variable set of flood-time and historical observations while maintaining competitive performance. The learned gates provide an adaptive mechanism for exploiting additional information when available without making those auxiliary observations mandatory at inference time.
